Joseph weeps when the brothers speak, rejects their fear, says he will provide for them and their children, and comforts them.
Jacob’s sons carry him to Canaan and bury him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field Abraham acquired as a burial holding, with Leah also named among those buried there.
After the mourning period, Joseph asks Pharaoh’s household to convey his oath-bound request to bury Jacob in Canaan; Pharaoh grants permission.
Genesis ends with Joseph's death in Egypt while preserving an expectation that God will bring Abraham's family to the promised land.
Joseph says God will visit Israel and bring them up to the promised land, makes the family swear to carry up his bones, dies at 110, is embalmed, and is placed in a coffin in Egypt.
The brothers send Joseph a message that Jacob had commanded him to forgive their transgression and sin; Genesis has not independently narrated Jacob giving that instruction.
The procession mourns at the threshing floor of Atad beyond the Jordan; the location receives the name Abel-mizraim in the narrative explanation.
Joseph weeps over Jacob, physicians embalm him for forty days, and Egypt mourns him for seventy days.
Pharaoh’s officials, elders, household members, chariots, horsemen, and family accompany Joseph toward Canaan.
Joseph lives to 110, sees Ephraim’s children to the third generation, and sees children of Machir son of Manasseh.
The narrative says physicians embalmed Jacob at Joseph’s direction, without calling him a king or describing a complete royal funerary protocol.
Genesis moves from universal origins in chapters 1-11 to the ancestral family narratives in chapters 12-50 and ends with Jacob's household in Egypt.
